desc:
Simulate a stack that can also remove its largest value. You are given a list ops of operations; each is a pair [type, x]:

  • [0, x]: push the value x on top. Produces no output.
  • [1, 0]: pop the top element and output it.
  • [2, 0]: output the top element without removing it.
  • [3, 0]: output the largest element in the stack without removing it.
  • [4, 0]: remove the largest element and output it. If several elements share the maximum value, remove the one closest to the top.

Return the outputs of all operations of types 1 to 4, in order. Operations of types 1 to 4 are only given when the stack is not empty.

Example: [[0,5],[0,1],[0,5],[3,0],[4,0],[1,0],[2,0]]: the stack is [5,1,5]; the largest is 5 (output 5); removing the maximum removes the top 5 (output 5), leaving [5,1]; pop outputs 1; top outputs 5. The answer is [5, 5, 1, 5].
constraints: type is in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}; for types other than 0 the second value is 0
Types 1 to 4 are only used on a non-empty stack
At least one operation produces an output
hints: A plain list makes every operation except push O(1) at best, but removing the maximum from the middle is O(n). With 3,000 operations that is fine, but can you do better?
You need fast access to both the top and the maximum, and an element removed through one route must disappear from the other.

Give every pushed element a unique id. Keep a stack and a max-heap of (value, id), plus a set of removed ids. When reading either structure, first discard entries whose id is in the removed set (lazy deletion).
editorial: Two structures describe the same set of elements: a stack ordered by time and a max-heap ordered by (value, push order). Push puts the element in both. Pop removes from the stack and popMax removes from the heap, so each must tell the other. We do that lazily: removed ids go into a set, and before reading the top of either structure we discard entries with removed ids.

Heap entries are (-value, -id) so that the largest value comes first, and among equal values the largest id, i.e. the one pushed latest (closest to the top). Since stack position and push order agree, that is the element nearest the top. Each element is added once and discarded at most once from each structure, so the total is O(n log n) time and O(n) space. A balanced doubly linked list with a sorted map of values gives the same bounds without lazy deletion.
